policy.concepts: Hierarchy and terms support discovery; adjacency never proves theological equivalence.
policy.names: Name assertions are source-, language-, and period-scoped. Contextual identification, translation, association, and conflation remain relationships, never automatic aliases.
policy.occurrences: Each occurrence identifies its source and locator; composite text records are not represented as single physical witnesses.
policy.classification: Conflict causes and conversion modes require evidence. Religious participation does not by itself make a conflict religious, and conquest does not by itself prove forced conversion.

concepts.label: Religion & worldview
concepts.description: Comparative root for beliefs, practices, institutions, experiences, and worldviews studied in their historical and cultural settings; membership never implies doctrinal equivalence.

concepts.label: Cosmology, origins & world order
concepts.description: Narratives and doctrines that explain how a world begins, is structured, and is sustained within a particular tradition.

concepts.label: Divine & more-than-human beings
concepts.description: Historically situated categories for deities, spirits, ancestors, adversarial beings, and reported encounters with them.

concepts.label: Personhood, agency & the human condition
concepts.description: Models of selfhood, embodiment, agency, identity, moral condition, and lived vulnerability across cultures and traditions.

concepts.label: Death, afterlife & eschatology
concepts.description: Teachings and narratives about dying, postmortem states, judgment, renewed life, and final or cyclical futures.

concepts.label: Revelation, knowledge & authority
concepts.description: Ways communities claim, transmit, authorize, interpret, and contest religious knowledge and authoritative texts.

concepts.label: Salvation, liberation & transformation
concepts.description: Tradition-specific accounts of release, awakening, reconciliation, purification, healing, and transformed life.

concepts.label: Ethics, law & social order
concepts.description: Norms, institutions, relationships, power, conflict, and material conditions that organize communal life.

concepts.label: Ritual, practice & experience
concepts.description: Patterned actions, disciplines, rites, and reported experiences through which people enact or encounter religious worlds.

concepts.label: Sacred place, time & community
concepts.description: Spatial, temporal, and communal forms through which sacred significance and collective belonging are organized.

concepts.label: Creation
concepts.description: Accounts of how a world, beings, or an ordered cosmos comes to exist; creators, sequence, and genre vary by source.

concepts.label: Cosmology
concepts.description: Models of the cosmos and its ordering principles, including relations among divine, human, and natural domains.

concepts.label: Flood
concepts.description: Flood narratives and doctrines treated in their own textual and historical settings rather than as one universal event.

concepts.label: Monotheism
concepts.description: Belief or worship centered on one deity, with the deity's identity and the treatment of other beings defined by each tradition.

concepts.label: Polytheism
concepts.description: Religious systems recognizing a plurality of deities whose number, rank, and relationships differ across sources.

concepts.label: Non-theism
concepts.description: Religious or philosophical frameworks that do not make a creator deity or supreme god their organizing premise.

concepts.label: Divine Council
concepts.description: Assemblies of deities or divine beings whose membership, authority, and function must be established source by source.

concepts.label: Divine Beings
concepts.description: Broad discovery category for beings treated as divine in a cited tradition; it never supplies a universal definition of divinity.

concepts.label: Gods
concepts.description: Named or classed deities documented within the language, period, and practices of a particular community.

concepts.label: Angels
concepts.description: Messenger or heavenly beings in traditions that use an angel category, without extending that label to unrelated beings elsewhere.

concepts.label: Demons
concepts.description: Adversarial, dangerous, or otherwise classified spirit beings whose status and moral character differ across traditions.

concepts.label: Evil
concepts.description: Moral, metaphysical, and experiential accounts of wrongdoing, harm, disorder, or opposition to an understood good.

concepts.label: Spirit
concepts.description: Source-language categories for breath, wind, incorporeal agency, or spirit, with no presumption that their semantic ranges coincide.

concepts.label: Ancestors
concepts.description: Deceased forebears addressed, remembered, or treated as continuing agents in particular social and ritual settings.

concepts.label: Possession
concepts.description: Claims that a spirit or other agent inhabits, controls, or speaks through a person, interpreted within local diagnostic systems.

concepts.label: Exorcism
concepts.description: Rites intended to expel, restrain, or negotiate with an afflicting being or force according to a tradition's own categories.

concepts.label: Miracles
concepts.description: Reported extraordinary events understood as signs or acts of divine agency, with evidential and doctrinal interpretation kept explicit.

concepts.label: Soul
concepts.description: Tradition-specific models of life, self, or enduring personhood; nefesh, ātman, psychē, ba, and similar terms are not automatic synonyms.

concepts.label: Consciousness
concepts.description: Accounts of subjective awareness and its relation to mind, body, self, and disciplined experience.

concepts.label: Mind
concepts.description: Concepts of cognition, intention, attention, and mental cultivation expressed through different philosophical and religious vocabularies.

concepts.label: Free will
concepts.description: Debates about whether and how agents control choices, bear responsibility, or act under causal, divine, or karmic conditions.

concepts.label: Destiny
concepts.description: Claims about allotted, foreknown, conditioned, or fated courses of life, distinguished from later retrospective interpretations.

concepts.label: Karma
concepts.description: Causal accounts linking action and consequence in South Asian traditions, with mechanisms and ethical meanings varying by school.

concepts.label: Sin
concepts.description: Tradition-specific concepts of wrongdoing, estrangement, transgression, or damaged relation to divine and communal norms.

concepts.label: Suffering
concepts.description: Experiences and explanations of pain, loss, dissatisfaction, or affliction, including doctrines about causes and responses.

concepts.label: Birth
concepts.description: Biological and socially recognized beginnings of personhood, including rites and doctrines that assign status or meaning to birth.

concepts.label: Gender
concepts.description: Culturally and historically organized identities, roles, and power relations associated with gender; sources must identify their own categories.

concepts.label: Sexuality
concepts.description: Culturally situated desires, practices, identities, and norms concerning sexual life and embodiment.

concepts.label: Afterlife
concepts.description: Any tradition-specific account of continued existence, renewed life, judgment, or postmortem condition after bodily death.

concepts.label: Resurrection
concepts.description: Restoration or transformation of the dead to life in traditions that teach resurrection, distinguished from rebirth and reincarnation.

concepts.label: Reincarnation
concepts.description: Accounts in which a person, self, or soul takes another embodied life; the continuing subject must be defined by the cited tradition.

concepts.label: Rebirth
concepts.description: Renewed conditioned existence across lives, especially Buddhist accounts that do not require an enduring soul.

concepts.label: Death
concepts.description: The end of embodied life together with the biological, social, ritual, and doctrinal meanings assigned to it.

concepts.label: Judgment
concepts.description: Evaluation of persons or acts by divine, postmortem, or eschatological authority in a specified source tradition.

concepts.label: Heaven
concepts.description: Tradition-specific heavenly realms, divine presence, or blessed postmortem states; imagery and conditions are not universalized.

concepts.label: Hell
concepts.description: Tradition-specific realms or states of punishment, exclusion, or suffering after death, whether temporary or final.

concepts.label: Underworld
concepts.description: Realms of the dead located below or apart from the living world in particular cosmologies and narratives.

concepts.label: Purgatory
concepts.description: The Catholic doctrine of final purification after death, not a generic label for every intermediate or punitive afterlife state.

concepts.label: Apocalypse
concepts.description: Revelatory literature or teaching that discloses cosmic crisis, judgment, or transformed order; modern catastrophe usage is secondary.

concepts.label: Prophecy
concepts.description: Speech, writing, or action presented as conveying divine communication, warning, interpretation, or foretelling in a stated context.

concepts.label: Revelation
concepts.description: Claims that otherwise unavailable truth is disclosed by divine or transcendent agency through text, event, vision, or experience.

concepts.label: Wisdom
concepts.description: Teachings and practices presented as skilled, insightful, or rightly ordered understanding of life and reality.

concepts.label: Knowledge
concepts.description: Claims, methods, and standards for knowing within religious and philosophical traditions, including reason, testimony, and experience.

concepts.label: Hidden Knowledge
concepts.description: Teachings represented as secret, esoteric, initiatory, or restricted, with access conditions and provenance recorded.

concepts.label: Authority
concepts.description: Recognized power to teach, interpret, command, authenticate, or govern within a community and historical setting.

concepts.label: Scripture
concepts.description: Texts a community treats as sacred or normatively authoritative, with boundaries and interpretive status established historically.

concepts.label: Canon
concepts.description: A historically formed set of texts, rules, or authoritative decisions recognized as normative by a community.

concepts.label: Heresy
concepts.description: A classification applied by authorities or communities to teachings judged outside accepted doctrinal boundaries; actor and period must be named.

concepts.label: Salvation
concepts.description: Tradition-specific rescue, reconciliation, healing, or fulfilled relation to an ultimate good; the problem being solved must be stated.

concepts.label: Liberation
concepts.description: Release from bondage, ignorance, cyclic existence, oppression, or another specified condition in religious and philosophical traditions.

concepts.label: Enlightenment
concepts.description: Awakening, illumination, or perfected insight in traditions that use such a goal, with the source term and path retained.

concepts.label: Forgiveness
concepts.description: Release from blame, debt, resentment, or divine condemnation in a specified interpersonal, communal, or theological setting.

concepts.label: Mercy
concepts.description: Compassionate restraint, aid, or pardon shown by a human or divine agent in a concrete moral and doctrinal context.

concepts.label: Mysticism
concepts.description: Practices and reports oriented toward direct, unitive, or otherwise extraordinary religious experience, interpreted within their traditions.

concepts.label: Healing
concepts.description: Practices or claims of bodily, psychological, social, or spiritual restoration whose methods and agents are documented locally.

concepts.label: Law
concepts.description: Codified or customary norms backed by recognized authority, including religious law when a source identifies it as such.

concepts.label: Ethics
concepts.description: Reflection and practice concerning right action, character, obligation, and good life within philosophical, religious, and social traditions.

concepts.label: Justice
concepts.description: Principles and institutions for fair treatment, right distribution, accountability, or restored relations in a stated society or tradition.

concepts.label: Violence
concepts.description: Physical, structural, or symbolic harm documented with actors, targets, and context; religious labels require evidence of religious causation or meaning.

concepts.label: War
concepts.description: Organized armed conflict analyzed through its political, ethical, and, where supported, religious causes and justifications.

concepts.label: Peace
concepts.description: Conditions and practices of nonwar, reconciliation, nonviolence, or just social relation, defined by the relevant actors and tradition.

concepts.label: Wealth
concepts.description: Material resources, property, exchange, and prosperity as organized and morally evaluated within a society or religious tradition.

concepts.label: Poverty
concepts.description: Material deprivation and unequal access to resources, including religious interpretations and responses only where sources document them.

concepts.label: Sacred Kingship
concepts.description: Forms of rule in which royal authority is constituted through divine descent, ritual office, or sacred legitimation in a specific polity.

concepts.label: Marriage
concepts.description: Socially recognized unions and their legal, kinship, ritual, economic, and religious dimensions across cultures.

concepts.label: Family
concepts.description: Culturally defined relations of kinship, care, descent, household, and obligation rather than a single universal household form.

concepts.label: Ritual
concepts.description: Repeated or formally patterned action carrying recognized social, symbolic, or religious meaning for participants.

concepts.label: Sacrifice
concepts.description: Offerings, transfers, renunciations, or killings performed for specified recipients and purposes in a ritual system.

concepts.label: Prayer
concepts.description: Address, petition, praise, confession, contemplation, or other communication directed within a religious framework.

concepts.label: Fasting
concepts.description: Deliberate restriction of food or drink for ritual, ethical, ascetic, commemorative, or disciplinary purposes.

concepts.label: Purity
concepts.description: Rules and practices distinguishing clean, unclean, fit, restricted, or consecrated states in a particular system.

concepts.label: Initiation
concepts.description: Rites that admit, transform, authorize, or mark transition into a group, status, office, or body of knowledge.

concepts.label: Magic
concepts.description: Practices intended to act through nonordinary powers or correspondences, described with local terminology and without ranking traditions.

concepts.label: Divination
concepts.description: Techniques for obtaining guidance or hidden information through signs, lots, specialists, texts, or inspired states.

concepts.label: Meditation
concepts.description: Disciplines of attention, contemplation, visualization, recitation, or awareness whose methods and goals vary by tradition.

concepts.label: Sacred Geography
concepts.description: Places, landscapes, routes, and spatial relations invested with sacred meaning by communities in particular histories.

concepts.label: Sacred Time
concepts.description: Calendars, festivals, commemorations, cycles, and exceptional moments that communities distinguish from ordinary time.

concepts.label: Community
concepts.description: Groups constituted or sustained through shared identity, practice, institution, memory, or sacred commitment.

concepts.label: Pilgrimage
concepts.description: Journey to a sacred destination or along a sacred route, documented through its participants, purposes, and ritual setting.

conceptEdges.rationale: Origin narratives, accounts of cosmic order, and models of ultimate reality need a shared browse axis while retaining their different literary and doctrinal settings.
Comparative anthropology distinguishes named deities, spirits, ancestors, and other supernatural agents, so this branch gathers their records without treating the categories as universal equivalents.
Accounts of mind, soul, freedom, identity, and suffering all concern what a person is and can do, although their source vocabularies remain distinct.
Death, postmortem destiny, and end-time transformation form a coherent comparison area, but tradition-specific afterlives must not be merged into one scheme.
Prophecy, revelation, scripture, and canon all concern how knowledge becomes authoritative, while philosophy of religious knowledge marks the evidential questions involved.
Practices and doctrines of release or transformation can be compared here only with explicit attention to each tradition's stated problem and goal.
Religious ethics intersects with law, political authority, kinship, violence, and economic life, making social order a distinct but internally diverse comparison axis.
Rites, prayer, divination, meditation, and related disciplines are forms of practice and experience whose meanings depend on performers and settings.
Sacred geography, calendars, pilgrimage, and community formation connect space and time with collective religious identity.
Creation is primarily an origins category because it addresses the coming-to-be of a world or its inhabitants.
Cosmology belongs under world order because it describes the structure and governing pattern of a cosmos.
Flood traditions commonly explain destruction, renewal, or reordered human life and therefore sit with origins and world-order narratives.
Monotheism is a model of divine order and ultimate reality, not merely a count detached from theology.
Polytheism organizes a cosmos through multiple divine agents and is therefore indexed with models of world order.
Non-theism marks a contrasting account of ultimate order and prevents the cosmology branch from assuming that all traditions are theistic.
A divine council depicts cosmic governance and belongs primarily with accounts of world order, while its members remain separately indexed as beings.
This umbrella concept directly names the branch's core subject while leaving local ontologies intact.
Gods are placed with divine beings because sources treat them as agents with superhuman power, identity, or cultic roles.
Angels are more-than-human agents in their source traditions and require a narrower record than the general divine-being category.
Demon classifications concern more-than-human agents, but their meanings cannot be inferred from a single later demonology.
Evil is placed here for its frequent personification or relation to adversarial powers, while a secondary link records its bearing on human agency.
Spirit is primarily grouped with more-than-human being categories while source-scoped terms preserve broader meanings such as breath or wind.
Ancestors can function as more-than-human social agents, while their kinship and community relations remain essential context.
Possession centers an encounter between human and more-than-human agency and is therefore anchored in this branch.
Exorcism presupposes a source-specific account of an afflicting agent, linking the rite primarily to more-than-human beings.
Miracles are indexed here because they are claims about divine or supernatural action in the world.
Soul concepts primarily address what a person is and what, if anything, persists through change or death.
Consciousness belongs with personhood because it concerns the character and continuity of lived awareness.
Mind is a faculty or dimension of persons and agents, even where a tradition rejects a permanent self.
Free will is placed under agency because it directly concerns control over action and moral responsibility.
Destiny qualifies the scope of personal agency by asking how far a life course is fixed or directed.
Karma directly joins human action to experienced condition and future consequence, making it a central agency concept.
Sin describes a moral condition or act attributed to persons, while its legal and ethical dimensions receive a secondary link.
Suffering is a feature of the human condition that many traditions make central to diagnosis and transformation.
Birth marks entry into embodied and social personhood, while communal recognition is represented by a secondary link.
Gender shapes lived personhood and agency rather than serving as a timeless biological or religious constant.
Sexuality is indexed with the human condition because it concerns embodiment, identity, relationship, and moral agency.
Afterlife is the branch's broad postmortem category and must retain distinct models rather than merging them.
Resurrection directly concerns postmortem or eschatological renewed life and therefore belongs in this branch.
Reincarnation is a postmortem continuity model and is kept distinct from Buddhist rebirth and Christian resurrection.
Rebirth is a cyclic postmortem process and remains separate from doctrines centered on a transmigrating self.
Death is the threshold around which afterlife and eschatological claims are organized.
Judgment determines or explains postmortem destiny in many eschatological systems and therefore sits primarily here.
Heaven is a named afterlife or eschatological destination in traditions that teach it.
Hell is indexed as an afterlife and judgment category while sources determine duration, inhabitants, and purpose.
Underworld concepts organize the location and condition of the dead, making them primarily postmortem categories.
Purgatory is placed here as a specifically defined postmortem purification doctrine.
Apocalypse primarily concerns final or transformative horizons of history and cosmos.
Prophecy is a claimed channel of revealed knowledge whose authority must be evaluated within its community and text.
Revelation directly concerns the acquisition and authorization of religious knowledge.
Wisdom is a mode of religious knowledge oriented toward discernment and practice rather than mere information.
Knowledge is the broad epistemic category under which revelation and other authorized ways of knowing can be compared.
Hidden knowledge is a restricted mode of transmitting purported truth and therefore belongs primarily with knowledge and authority.
Authority determines whose texts, interpretations, and institutions can define accepted religious knowledge.
Scripture is a durable medium through which claimed revelation and teaching receive communal authority.
Canon records the boundary-making process by which some texts or rulings receive authoritative status.
Heresy is indexed here because it is produced through contested claims to doctrinal authority and knowledge.
Salvation names a goal of decisive religious transformation while leaving its agent and mechanism source-specific.
Liberation is grouped here because it describes freedom from a diagnosed condition, though Hindu, Buddhist, and social meanings differ.
Enlightenment is a transformation of understanding and condition rather than a universal synonym for salvation.
Forgiveness changes a damaged moral or religious relationship and therefore belongs among forms of reconciliation.
Mercy is indexed as a means or expression of restorative transformation without assuming one theology of grace.
Mysticism belongs here when experience is understood as transformative, while its practices also receive a ritual secondary link.
Healing is a form of restoration and transformation, even when its ritual performance also warrants a practice link.
Law structures permitted action and institutional order, making it a primary social-order concept.
Ethics is the branch's central normative category and must remain distinguishable from law and custom.
Justice evaluates social rules, distributions, and remedies, so it belongs primarily with ethics and social order.
Violence affects social order and moral evaluation, while its religious role must be demonstrated rather than assumed.
War is a collective institution of violence and political order rather than an automatically religious event.
Peace belongs with social order as both a political condition and an ethical aim.
Wealth shapes social hierarchy and ethical obligation and therefore belongs in the social-order branch.
Poverty is a material and distributive condition central to inequality and ethical social analysis.
Sacred kingship joins political authority with religious legitimation and belongs primarily under social order.
Marriage organizes rights, alliance, household, and descent, making it primarily a social-order and kinship concept.
Family is a foundational institution of social organization, with sacred and communal dimensions recorded separately.
Ritual is the branch's broad action category and supplies context for more specific rites and disciplines.
Sacrifice is a structured ritual act whose material, agent, recipient, and aim must be documented.
Prayer is a recurring religious practice and reported mode of relation to divine or sacred agents.
Fasting is an embodied discipline whose timing and purpose are defined through practice.
Purity categories are enacted and maintained through ritual practice rather than assumed to be universal hygiene rules.
Initiation is a ritual transition whose sequence and social effects are essential evidence.
Magic is indexed as a practice category because its techniques, objects, and intended effects are performed and learned.
Divination is a procedural practice of seeking knowledge, so its primary home is ritual even when it informs authority.
Meditation is primarily a cultivated practice and experience, with a secondary link to transformative goals.
Sacred geography directly organizes religious significance in space and therefore anchors the place dimension of this branch.
Sacred time organizes collective memory and practice through recurring or singular temporal boundaries.
Community is the social setting in which sacred places, times, texts, and practices receive shared recognition.
Pilgrimage joins sacred geography with communal movement and is therefore placed primarily under place and community.
Creation accounts may be presented as revealed teaching or authoritative sacred narrative, so they also belong in revelation discovery.
Cosmological models are often transmitted through authoritative texts or teachings, making their claimed source of knowledge relevant.
A council is a form of cosmic governance, but its participants are also individually or collectively classified as divine beings.
Accounts of evil also address human wrongdoing, responsibility, suffering, and the limits of agency.
Spirit vocabularies can describe breath, life, or a dimension of personhood as well as more-than-human agents.
Ancestors remain embedded in kin groups, remembered places, and communal rites rather than functioning only as isolated spirit beings.
Possession is commonly recognized, managed, or contested through embodied practice, diagnosis, and ritual performance.
Exorcism is enacted as a rite or specialized practice even though its target belongs to a more-than-human ontology.
Miracle reports can function as signs that authorize a messenger, doctrine, or revelation, so their evidential role is indexed here.
Karma links action and consequence through moral causation and therefore bears directly on ethical conduct.
Sin is evaluated against moral, legal, or communal norms as well as being described as a personal condition.
Many paths of liberation or salvation begin by diagnosing suffering and proposing its cessation or transformation.
Birth becomes communal status through kinship recognition, naming, calendars, and rites of transition.
Judgment applies standards of conduct and responsibility, joining postmortem destiny to ethics and normative order.
Apocalyptic discourse claims to disclose hidden or future realities, making revelation a necessary secondary context.
Some prophecy concerns judgment, death, or future transformation, although prediction is not required for every prophetic act.
Restricted knowledge may be conferred through initiation or cultivated through specialized practices and experiences.
Religious authority also structures offices, law, governance, and permitted conduct within communities.
A canon exists through communal recognition and helps maintain shared memory and identity across time.
Heresy classifications can carry legal, political, and social consequences beyond doctrinal disagreement.
Mystical reports are often connected with contemplative disciplines, bodily techniques, or other repeatable practices.
Healing may be sought or enacted through prayer, laying on of hands, specialists, medicines, or ritual procedures.
Sacred rule is performed through courts, temples, territories, festivals, and communities that recognize royal sacrality.
Marriage rites and kinship alliances establish communal membership and continuity as well as social obligations.
Families carry shared memory, household observance, ancestry, and belonging across generations.
Pilgrimage is a journey to sacred place and also a patterned bodily and communal practice.
Meditative disciplines are frequently directed toward awakening, liberation, purification, or other stated transformations.

conflictCases.name: Thirty Years' War
actors: Catholic, Lutheran, and Calvinist Imperial estates
Holy Roman emperors of the House of Habsburg
conflictCases.summary: A changing series of wars in which confessional alignments interacted with territorial ambitions and interstate competition.
conflictCases.statedCause: There was no single stated cause shared by every belligerent: confessional defense, territorial acquisition, and geopolitical predominance appear in different actors' documented aims.
participantJustifications: Catholic, Lutheran, and Calvinist rulers presented parts of the struggle through confessional allegiance.
Denmark entered while seeking German territory after losses elsewhere.
France supported the Protestant side primarily to pursue political predominance against Habsburg power.
scholarlyInterpretations: OpenStax treats the war as part of the European wars of religion while explicitly identifying territorial and political motives for particular intervening states.
The Westphalia settlement addressed ecclesiastical liberty alongside territorial, dynastic, and constitutional disputes, demonstrating that the conflict cannot be reduced to one causal axis.
conflictCases.disputedCausation: The relative weight of religion and state interest changes by belligerent and phase; Atlas does not label every action in the war as religiously caused.
conflictCases.uncertainty: These assignments describe evidenced case-level motives and settlement issues, not a uniform motive held by every soldier, ruler, or population.

conflictCases.name: Indian Rebellion of 1857
actors: Bengal Army sepoys and other rebels
Dispossessed or threatened Indian rulers and elites
Indian Hindu and Muslim communities represented in the cited sources
conflictCases.summary: A rebellion against East India Company rule with military, anti-colonial, political, and religious grievances whose relative weight varied among participants.
conflictCases.statedCause: Contemporary records repeatedly identify the cartridge controversy as an immediate trigger, while also naming annexation, military discipline, missionary activity, and opposition to foreign rule as wider grievances.
participantJustifications: Contemporary Indian press extracts framed the cartridge orders and colonial policy as threats to religion and caste.
Indian opponents of Company rule sought self-government or the restoration of displaced authority.
Company and British parliamentary accounts disputed whether cartridges were the sole cause and acknowledged pre-existing grievances.
scholarlyInterpretations: OpenStax presents the rebellion as an attempt to overthrow British rule and connects it to direct colonial administration, elite dispossession, missionary activity, and the cartridge crisis.
The National Archives dossier preserves competing contemporary explanations rather than treating one participant account as a complete causal history.
conflictCases.disputedCausation: Sources disagree over whether greased-cartridge fears were a sole cause, an immediate trigger, or one grievance among broader anti-colonial and political causes.
conflictCases.uncertainty: The labels mutiny and rebellion encode different scopes and perspectives; this record uses rebellion while retaining the source terminology and does not impute one motive to all participants.

conflictCauseAssignments.evidence: The cited history situates the war among conflicts between Catholic and Protestant states and identifies Catholic, Lutheran, and Calvinist combatants in the Empire.
OpenStax identifies Denmark's hope of gaining German territory, while the peace treaty resolves named territorial possessions and cessions.
OpenStax states that Catholic France joined the Protestant side primarily to become Europe's preeminent power, evidence against an exclusively confessional classification.
The case evidence documents confessional alignment, territorial acquisition, and interstate power goals operating within the same conflict.
OpenStax describes the rebellion as an attempt to overthrow British rule and places it within resistance to foreign domination.
The sources document objections to missionary activity and fears that the cartridge order threatened Hindu and Muslim religious observance and caste status.
The cited account connects resistance to direct Company government, the doctrine of lapse, annexation, and Indian elites' loss of authority.
Case sources jointly document colonial rule, annexation, military grievances, missionary concerns, and the cartridge crisis rather than a single sufficient cause.
The National Archives dossier assembles contemporary accounts that assign different causal weight to cartridge fears, religion, aggression, and other grievances.

conversionCases.name: Constantinian legalization and sponsorship of Christianity
conversionCases.summary: A change in Christianity's legal and institutional position under imperial government; this case does not claim a forced mass conversion or make Christianity the state religion in 313.
conversionCases.statedPolicy: The 313 policy granted religious choice and restored Christian property; Constantine's later government privileged and institutionally supported Christianity.
conversionCases.statedJustification: The edict presents religious liberty and restoration as serving public peace and divine favor, while the later imperial program linked Christian institutions to governance.
conversionCases.resistanceContinuity: The 313 settlement allowed traditional religious practices to continue even as Christianity acquired legal rights, property, patronage, and growing institutional influence.
conversionCases.disputesUncertainty: Constantine's personal beliefs and their chronology are debated; Atlas records observable policy and patronage and does not infer that the population converted because the emperor favored Christianity.

conversionCases.name: Safavid establishment and spread of Twelver Shiism in Iran
conversionCases.summary: A state-backed religious transformation that included documented direct coercion in its early phase and a longer, uneven process of institution building and adoption.
conversionCases.statedPolicy: Shah Ismail declared Twelver Shiism the state religion and ordered Sunni subjects to adopt it while the state funded Shia schools and shrines.
conversionCases.statedJustification: The cited account describes a policy intended to unify subjects and distinguish the new Safavid state from Sunni Ottoman and Uzbek rivals.
conversionCases.resistanceContinuity: Sources document conversion-or-exile demands, lethal punishment for some resistance, and continuing Sunni presence; persistence and later adoption varied over time and place.
conversionCases.disputesUncertainty: Scholarship disputes any claim of instantaneous, uniform conversion. Direct early coercion is documented, but Atlas does not attribute every later Shia affiliation solely to force.

conversionModeAssignments.evidence: The historical overview documents restored property and legal rights, privileged status, imperial church councils, and government advocacy of Christianity.
The 313 policy granted religious choice, and the cited historical account states that traditional Roman practices could continue during the initial legalization of Christianity.
The Safavid state declared Twelver Shiism official, funded schools and shrines, and brought Shia scholars into Iran.
The source states that Shah Ismail ordered Sunni Muslims to become Shia and that people who resisted conversion while remaining in Iran faced death.
Sunni clerics were presented with conversion or exile, and resistance by those who remained could be punished by death.
The policy imposed conversion, exile, or lethal consequences on Sunni subjects while funding institutions of the favored Twelver Shia establishment.
Peer-reviewed scholarship challenges an overnight-conversion model and documents that Sunnism survived and was still subject to persecution in the seventeenth century.
